label: January–December 1881
atlas_dek: The episodes reported from January through December 1881 in our dossiers that involve anti-Black violence or threats, placed on 1910 county lines and by month (some events were first reported the month after). Lynchings of white, Mexican and Chinese victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers but not on the map. Hover for a short summary; select a dot to read the account in the sidebar. Drafts: no entry has had human review.
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 437 episodes reported from January through December 1881. These months cover two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white, Mexican, Italian and Chinese victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are therefore included here, unlike in our other months. The episodes come from the located events in each month’s table, which include events from the month before that were first reported later; from the Monroe Work Today inventory, our only lynching list for this year; and from a check for attacks by one person (a separate pass over every article for July and August, part of the first screen for January through June). Each month’s search also read the following month’s papers for more on known episodes, and December’s read January 1882. For 1881 the search used white papers only. January also holds events from late December 1880 that were first reported in January; they are marked as falling before the year. Older 1880 events that 1881 papers recalled, among them testimony on violence at the November 1880 election, are held for a separate 1880 collection.

We wrote 528 dossiers; 91 are set aside, and 32 more events got no dossier because the table alone showed them out of scope. Set aside: nine lawful acts reported as violence (six legal executions, among them Henry Lawson at Chattanooga, the man a July mob had tried to lynch, and three whippings ordered by the mayor at the Alexandria police station); twenty-six duplicates; four events from other months; anti-Black-scope events in which no report gives anyone’s race and no lynching was involved (twenty); events with no force, two-sided fights, reports a contemporary source denied, rumors and forecasts of lynchings where no crowd gathered, threatened lynchings of Black prisoners by Black crowds, an attempt to free two prisoners from a jail, and joke items from Tombstone, Deadwood and Kentucky.

Some episodes run over several days and towns. Where a pursuit moved from one jail to another, as with John Taylor in North Carolina in June, each raid is its own entry and the entries link to one another; the victim is counted once, at the lynching.

Inventory differences are kept and noted, not counted: Perry Thompson in Sharkey County, Mississippi, whom the inventory lists as lynched and the papers describe as killed when hidden men fired on Black men walking to a political meeting; and Juarique and Sanchez near El Paso in April, whom the inventory lists as lynched and the papers describe as shot by Americans in a quarrel over land. The inventory’s thirteen victims at Las Animas are set aside: the papers place a robbery ambush of Mexican traders in Sonora, Mexico.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over an arrest or a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights and threats with no force stay in the reader but out of the totals; manhunts for an accused Black man with no capture reported are kept as an upper bound. Peonage, force used to hold a Black worker to labor, is always included.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched the papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. A coding agent (Sonnet) then read each dossier and recorded who acted, what they did and to whom; the type, the lynching stage and whether an episode counts are derived from those codes by fixed rules. Where the rules flag a hard case, a second coding agent reads the dossier independently, and cases where the two readings disagree are marked “Disputed coding.” White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: entries have not had human review, except the scope rulings noted in the codebook.
